title: Power Mean Limit Theorems: lim_{r→±∞} M_r(x)

problemStatement.formal: powerMean_tendsto_max : ∀ (hx : ∀ i, 0 < x i), Tendsto (fun r => ((∑ i, x i ^ r) / Fintype.card ι) ^ (1/r)) atTop (nhds (Finset.univ.sup' univ_nonempty x))
problemStatement.plain: For a finite collection of positive reals x₁,...,xₙ, the power mean M_r = ((∑ xᵢʳ)/n)^(1/r) converges to max(xᵢ) as r → +∞ and to min(xᵢ) as r → -∞. The +∞ direction uses a squeeze: max·n^(-1/r) ≤ M_r ≤ max with n^(-1/r) → 1. The -∞ direction uses duality: M_{-r}(x) = (M_r(1/x))⁻¹.
whyMatters: Completes the picture of power means: M_r interpolates between min, harmonic, geometric, arithmetic, and max
The squeeze theorem argument is the canonical proof of the max-limit
The duality M_{-r}(x) = (M_r(1/x))⁻¹ reduces the -∞ case to the +∞ case cleanly

proven: tendsto_M_atTop: M_r → max(xᵢ) as r → +∞ (squeeze theorem)
tendsto_M_atBot: M_r → min(xᵢ) as r → -∞ (via duality + composition with negation)
powerMean_tendsto_max: summary theorem for the +∞ limit
powerMean_tendsto_min: summary theorem for the -∞ limit

currentState.focus: 12 public theorems, 7 private helpers, 3 defs, 0 sorries, 0 axioms. Complete proof of both power mean limit theorems.

knowledge.progressSummary: COMPLETE: Proved lim_{r→+∞} M_r = max and lim_{r→-∞} M_r = min via squeeze theorem and duality.
